name: Penrose's Spherical Impulsive Wave
description: Flat spacetime cut along the future light cone of one event and joined again with a warp, which leaves a spherical gravitational wave one instant thick expanding at the speed of light. With the warp of a cosmic string it is the wave a string sends out when it snaps, with the cone of the string ahead of the wave and plain flat space behind it.
convention: The string's mass per unit length $\mu$ enters through $\beta = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$ and $k = (1 - \beta^2)/4$, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Roger Penrose's "cut and paste" method of 1972 makes a gravitational wave out of flat spacetime and a pair of scissors [penrose1972impulsive, podolsky2000snapping]. The cut runs along a null surface, such as the future light cone of one event, which is the history of a flash of light spreading from it, and the two pieces are attached again with a warp, each point of one side joined to a shifted point of the other [podolsky2000snapping]. Cut along a null plane, the method makes an impulsive wave with a plane front, the family that holds the shock of Peter Aichelburg and Roman Sexl [podolsky1999expanding, aichelburg1971]. Cut along a light cone, it makes a wave whose front is a sphere [podolsky1999expanding]. Spacetime is flat inside the sphere and flat outside it, and all of the curvature sits on the sphere itself, a shell of gravitational wave one instant thick [podolsky2000snapping].¶How do you warp a sphere? At any moment the wave front is a sphere, and stereographic projection lays a sphere out on a plane, each point named by one complex number $Z$ [podolsky2000snapping]. A warp is a map of that plane that keeps every angle, $Z \to h(Z)$ with $h$ a holomorphic function: the point $Z$ on the inside of the front is glued to the point $h(Z)$ on the outside [podolsky2000snapping]. Lorentz transformations are maps of this kind, $h = (aZ + b)/(cZ + d)$, and they are the only holomorphic maps that carry the whole sphere onto itself [podolsky2000snapping]. Any other $h$ leaves part of the outer sphere uncovered, and the gap is a physical object, such as the missing wedge around a cosmic string [podolsky2000snapping].¶Two flat pieces and a rule for gluing them make an awkward metric, so can it be written in one piece? It can: Yavuz Nutku and Penrose in 1992, and Peter Hogan in 1993, found coordinates in which the metric is continuous across the wave front [podolsky1999expanding, hogan1993]. In them $ds^2 = 2\left|V\,dZ + U\,\Theta(U)\,\bar H\,d\bar Z\right|^2 + 2\,dU\,dV$, with the front at $U = 0$ and the step $\Theta(U)$ equal to $1$ ahead of it and $0$ behind [podolsky2000snapping]. The function $H$ measures how far the warp is from a Lorentz transformation: it is the Schwarzian derivative $H = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[h'''/h' - \tfrac{3}{2}\left(h''/h'\right)^2\right]$, which no Lorentz transformation changes [podolsky2000snapping]. All of the curvature is in the kink at $U = 0$, a Dirac delta of strength $H/V$ on the front [podolsky2000snapping]. With the tie between these coordinates and the Lorentz group in hand, Hogan found further continuous charts in 1994, in one of which the fronts are the light cones of the points of a single world line [hogan1994, podolsky2000snapping].¶The simplest warp that is no Lorentz transformation is a power, $h = Z^\beta$ with $\beta < 1$ [podolsky2000snapping]. It squeezes the full turn $2\pi$ about the axis into $2\pi\beta$, so the flat space ahead of the wave is missing a wedge: it is the cone around a straight cosmic string, while behind the wave no string is left [podolsky2000snapping, vilenkin1981]. The string has snapped, and its two ends ride the wave front apart at the speed of light, each interpreted as a massless particle [podolsky2000snapping]. Reinaldo Gleiser and Jorge Pullin, asking in 1989 whether cosmic strings are gravitationally stable, matched two flat spacetimes across the cone and read the result as the gravitational wave from a string that splits [gleiser1989splitting, podolsky2000snapping]. That same year Jiří Bičák and Bernd Schmidt came to it from another side, as a limit of solutions with boost and rotation symmetry in which two null particles fly apart from one point [bicak1989, podolsky2000snapping]. Bičák's own reading in 1990 was of two half strings that approach at the speed of light and part again the instant they meet [bicak1990, podolsky2000snapping].¶What does the wave do to things in its path? The answer for free particles came in 2003 from Jiří Podolský and Roland Steinbauer, who followed them across the front [podolsky2003geodesics]. One case is easy to picture: a ring of particles at rest around the string, in the plane through the break and perpendicular to the string [podolsky2003geodesics]. The front reaches every particle of the ring at the same moment, and behind it each one moves straight toward the centre at the same speed, so the ring stays a circle and shrinks [podolsky2003geodesics]. A sphere of particles at rest loses its shape: behind the wave it is a more complicated surface, symmetric about the axis of the string [podolsky2003geodesics].¶Penrose had described his spherical waves as impulsive limits of the waves of Ivor Robinson and Andrzej Trautman, and the limit went unwritten until 1999, when Podolský and Jerry Griffiths took it explicitly [podolsky1999expanding, robinson1960]. In Robinson and Trautman's coordinates the limit leaves the square of a delta function in the metric, which a discontinuous change of coordinates removes [podolsky1999expanding]. They also carried the wave into de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space, after Hogan had set one in the de Sitter universe in 1992 [podolsky1999expanding, hogan1992]. A pair of strings can share one wave: in 2000 Podolský and Griffiths built the warp for two strings that collide and both snap where they meet, a case Nutku and Penrose had outlined [podolsky2000snapping]. A wave can also come in before it goes out, as in Hogan's solution of 1995, where one implodes onto an event and a second explodes from it [hogan1995].

related.text: Flat spacetime on both sides of the wave. Penrose cut it along the light cone of one event and glued the halves back with a warp [penrose1972impulsive, podolsky2000snapping].
The cone ahead of the wave. With the warp $h = Z^\beta$ the flat space outside the front is the string's, and the wave is what it sends out when it snaps [podolsky2000snapping].
Penrose's wave is the limit of a Robinson-Trautman wave of type N as its profile shrinks to an impulse [podolsky1999expanding].
Penrose's cut and paste along a null plane, where this one is cut along a light cone. The shock of a massless particle is one of the plane waves it makes [podolsky1999expanding, aichelburg1971].
The waves with plane fronts, whose impulsive members are the other kind Penrose's cut and paste makes [podolsky1999expanding].
An impulsive wave on a sphere that keeps its size, in de Sitter space, built by the same cut and paste along a cosmological horizon [podolsky1999nonexpanding].
Penrose's impulsive waves with plane fronts, two of them colliding head on. He and K. A. Khan found that exact spacetime in 1971 [khan1971].

coordinates.name: Null
domains: V\rho^2 = kU \;\text{(the string, ahead of the wave)}

parameters.description: Strength of the wave, $k = (1 - \beta^2)/4$, for a string of mass per unit length $\mu$ that leaves the fraction $\beta = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$ of the full angle around it
The step at the wave front, $1$ ahead of the wave, where $U > 0$, and $0$ behind it

coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $U$ and $V$, both lengths, with $\rho$ and $\phi$ polar coordinates on the stereographic plane $Z = \rho e^{i\phi}$ of the wave front $U = 0$, and $\mathrm{sgn}(U)$ is the sign of $U$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Retarded Spherical
domains: r\sin^2\theta = -2ku \;\text{(the string, ahead of the wave)}

parameters.description: Strength of the wave, $k = (1 - \beta^2)/4$, for a string of mass per unit length $\mu$ that leaves the fraction $\beta = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$ of the full angle around it
The step at the wave front, $1$ ahead of the wave, where $u < 0$, and $0$ behind it

coordinates.convention: We use a retarded coordinate $u$ and a radius $r$, both lengths, with $u = ct - r$ behind the wave for the inertial time $t$ there, $\theta$ measured from the string, and $\mathrm{sgn}(u)$ the sign of $u$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Behind the Wave
coordinates.convention: We use the inertial time $t$ and spherical coordinates $(r, \theta, \phi)$ about the event where the string snaps, with $\theta$ measured from the line the string lay along. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ahead of the Wave
domains: R^2 + z^2 = c^2T^2 \;\text{(the wave front, for } T > 0\text{, with the wave inside it)}

parameters.description: Fraction of the full angle left around the string, $\beta = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, so that the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - \beta)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, R, \phi, z)$ at rest with the string, with $T$ carrying dimensions of time, $R$ the proper distance from the string, and $z$ the proper length along it, and we take $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.
